title: Header files, declarations, include guards and organizing source files
learningObjectives: Distinguish a header's declarations and interface contract from source-file definitions and implementation details.
Create a conventional include guard that prevents repeated processing of the same header within one translation unit.
Explain why include guards do not prevent duplicate external definitions across separate translation units.
Place function prototypes, shared types and necessary macros in headers while keeping ordinary function and object definitions in one source file.
Use #include with quoted and angle-bracket forms appropriately and understand that inclusion is preprocessing rather than runtime loading.
Build a small multi-file C program and diagnose missing declarations, mismatched prototypes, duplicate definitions and unresolved external symbols.

understand.concept: A C program may be divided into translation units, usually one source file after preprocessing. Header files commonly declare interfaces shared across those units. An include directive inserts the header's contents into the including source during preprocessing; it does not dynamically load a module at runtime.
understand.whyItMatters: A clear header/source boundary makes larger C programs easier to compile, test and maintain. Incorrect header contents can cause duplicate definitions, inconsistent declarations and linker errors.
understand.analogy: A header is like a service contract: it tells other files which operations and types are available, while a source file provides the implementation.
understand.analogyLimit: A header is not a separately linked module and an include guard is not a linker mechanism. The preprocessor handles each translation unit independently.

explain.narrative:
A typical header contains declarations such as function prototypes, typedefs, enum and struct declarations, and carefully chosen macros. A corresponding .c file contains function definitions. Use an include guard such as `#ifndef PROJECT_GEOMETRY_H`, `#define PROJECT_GEOMETRY_H`, and `#endif`. Choose a distinctive macro name to avoid collisions.

Do not place ordinary external function definitions or externally linked object definitions in a header included by multiple source files; that can create multiple definitions at link time. A `static inline` function in a header is a different design with internal linkage and should be used intentionally. `#include "project.h"` typically searches the including file's directory and configured include paths before system paths; `#include <stdio.h>` requests a standard or implementation-provided header search. Exact search paths are toolchain configuration.

examples.title: A guarded header and one implementation file
examples.explanation: The header declares the function once per translation unit. geometry.c owns the external definition, and main.c includes the interface before calling it. Build the files together, for example: cc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic main.c geometry.c -o app. The combined listing is illustrative and should be split into the three named files.

examples.title: Use a header for a shared type and function prototype
examples.explanation: The header defines a shared type and declares the operation. The implementation includes its own header so the compiler checks that the function definition agrees with the public prototype. A complete project should include stddef.h or another suitable declaration for NULL, or use an explicit null-pointer comparison with an included standard header; this snippet needs #include <stddef.h> before compiling as a standalone translation unit.

practise.guidedTask: Split the first example into geometry.h, geometry.c and main.c. Compile and link all three source/header inputs as shown. Then remove the prototype from the header and observe the compiler diagnostic; next duplicate the function definition in a second .c file and inspect the linker error.
practise.independentTask: Design a two-module C program with a public header, one implementation file and a main file. Use an include guard, place each external definition in exactly one source file, and document the compile/link command.
hints: An include guard prevents repeated inclusion inside one translation unit; it does not coordinate different translation units.
Keep ordinary external function definitions in one .c file, not in a widely included header.
Include the public header from its implementation file so declarations and definitions are checked together.
A declaration tells the compiler about an entity; a definition provides the entity's implementation or storage.
A missing declaration is usually a compile-time issue; an unresolved external symbol is commonly a link-time issue.
Use distinctive guard names and include only the headers needed by the public interface.

questions.prompt: What is the primary role of a conventional header file?
options: To expose declarations and shared interface information to translation units.
To execute code when the program starts.
To store the final executable machine code.
To replace the linker.
questions.answer: To expose declarations and shared interface information to translation units.
questions.explanation: Headers communicate declarations, types and other interface material to source files that include them.

questions.prompt: What does an include guard prevent?
options: Repeated processing of the same guarded header within one translation unit.
All duplicate definitions across every source file in a program.
All linker errors.
Runtime loading of a header.
questions.answer: Repeated processing of the same guarded header within one translation unit.
questions.explanation: The guard macro is tracked during preprocessing of one translation unit; separate source files are preprocessed independently.

questions.prompt: Where should an ordinary externally linked function definition normally appear?
options: In one implementation source file (.c).
In every header that declares it.
In every source file that calls it.
Only in the Makefile.
questions.explanation: A single source file should own an ordinary external definition so the linker sees one definition for that entity.

options: During preprocessing, by inserting the header contents into the translation unit.
At runtime when the function is called.
During program termination.
Only by the linker after object files are created.
questions.answer: During preprocessing, by inserting the header contents into the translation unit.
questions.explanation: The preprocessor expands the include directive before normal compilation; it is not a runtime loading feature.

questions.prompt: Which command illustrates compiling and linking two implementation files together?
options: cc -std=c11 main.c geometry.c -o app
cc main.c -o app while geometry.c is never compiled or linked
run geometry.h
linker main.c geometry.h at runtime
questions.explanation: Both implementation source files must be compiled and linked into the final executable.
